claims.claim: On October 15, Citizen Lab published a technical investigation into **AdFection**: targeted advertising used to deliver zero-click mercenary spyware. Researchers linked Discover-Tech, an Israeli advertising company, to a pipeline connecting ordinary ad inventory with surveillance vendors. Their evidence includes attacks on devices at Al Jazeera in 2024 and 2025. The publication is new; those attacks are not happening for the first time this week.

claims.claim: The important story isn't that an evil banner can magically hack every phone. It's that the advertising system already supplies two things an attacker wants: a way to locate particular devices and a way to deliver code to them. Add a working exploit, and “I never clicked it” stops being the defense people assume it is.

claims.claim: Start with targeting. When an app or website offers an advertising slot, intermediaries can circulate information about the audience and device through a real-time auction. Depending on the implementation, that information can include advertising identifiers, IP addresses and location signals. Buyers decide which impressions to purchase.
unknowns: Documentary analysis of collaborating researchers, not an independent device examination or exploit replication.

claims.claim: Next comes delivery. An ad is not necessarily a flat picture. Its rendering can involve scripts, additional network requests and code from multiple companies. A recognizable publisher does not personally write every component that arrives through its advertising supply chain.

claims.claim: Then comes exploitation. **Running advertising JavaScript is not the same thing as compromising the operating system.** Installing spyware requires an additional attack against the target's software. That distinction matters: it separates a demonstrated infection from fingerprinting, reconnaissance or an ad impression.

claims.claim: [Citizen Lab's investigation](https://citizenlab.ca/research/how-discover-tech-turned-targeted-ads-into-a-pipeline-for-spyware/) describes Discover-Tech ads that contacted an intermediate server. That server could decide, using identifiers and the source IP address, whether to return further code. Non-targets could receive nothing. Selected devices could be sent onward into the spyware delivery process.

claims.claim: Citizen Lab reports that Discover-Tech appeared on approved or certified vendor lists maintained by Google and IAB Europe. Following disclosures, both removed it from their registries; other advertising companies also disconnected or restricted its access. These responses are recorded in Citizen Lab’s report and correspondence section.

claims.claim: Keep browsers and operating systems updated. Blocking ads and trackers can reduce exposure to this delivery channel; it cannot establish that a previously exposed device is clean or guarantee protection against every spyware route. Disabling advertising identifiers reduces one targeting input, not every possible identifier.

claims.claim: For organizations handling sensitive reporting, legal work or public-interest research, the question should be operational: which third-party advertising and tracking components are allowed on managed devices, and what evidence would reveal an unexpected chain of network connections? People at elevated risk need specialist security support, not just another reminder to inspect links.
